newsitem.title: USA: U. of Minnesota, feds in fight over drug sale.
newsitem.headline: U. of Minnesota, feds in fight over drug sale.

text.p: A ongoing battle between the University of Minnesota and the federal government over the sale of an experimental drug and the handling of federal research grants has landed the two parties in court.

According to the university, the U.S. Department of Justice put the school on notice last week that it intended to file suit by Dec 20 to recoop $100 million in drug sale and grant funds because of alleged fund abuses in the the school's department of surgery.
Last Friday, the university in a preemptive strike filed a lawsuit in federal court in Minneapolis.

The suit asks the court to void a designation the school received from the National Institutes of Health in 1995, restore the university's authority over federal research grants and declare that the federal government's claims agains the university were unconstitutional and based on unsound legal theories.
"The university has been forced to take action at this time after exhaustive attempts to avoid litigation," said university Board of Regents chair Tom Reagan in a statement released Monday.

"We believe the federal government is trying to use the (National Institutes of Health) designation as a lever to coerce the university into paying an outrageous settlement in order to shift state dollars into federal coffers."
Joe Krovisky, a spokesman for the Justice Department's civil division, declined to comment on the matter because of the lawsuit filed by the university.

Mike Nelson, the university's public relations representative, said the school had acknowledged that a "small fraction" of the grant money might have been mismanaged and that the school had been in settlement negotiations with the justice department over the matter.
The drug at issue -- Minnesota Antilymphocyte Globulin -- was developed by university surgeon John Najarian to aid transplant patients adapt to their new organs, Nelson said.

The drug program was discontinued in March 1994 following an 11-month internal investigation which revealed "gross abuses," according to a news release from the university. A year later, the university announced findings of grants management abuse in the department of surgery and took corrective action, the release said.

"When we found wrongdoing, we promptly investigated it, did the hard work of disclosing it and took the corrective action necessary," university president Nils Hasselmo said in a statement. "The government is wrong to now blame the university for problems it allowed to go unchecked while it slept on the solution."
